title: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
objectives: Use arithmetic operators correctly, including floor division and modulo with negative numbers.
Explain short-circuit evaluation and why and/or return operands rather than booleans.
Read chained comparisons and operator precedence without guessing.
Apply bitwise operators to classic interview tasks.
Use the walrus operator := and augmented assignment appropriately.
definition: An operator is a symbol or keyword that combines values (operands) into an expression that Python evaluates to a single object. Python groups operators into arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, identity, membership and assignment operators, and evaluates them according to fixed precedence and associativity rules.

theory.heading: Arithmetic: /, //, % and **
theory.body: The / operator always performs true division and returns a float, even for 6 / 3. Floor division // rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero, so -7 // 2 is -4. The modulo operator % is defined so that (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a, which means the result takes the sign of the divisor: -7 % 2 is 1. This differs from C and Java, and it is why Python's % is convenient for wrapping indices and clock arithmetic. divmod(a, b) returns both results at once.

theory.heading: Comparison and chaining
theory.body: Comparisons return True or False and can be chained: a < b < c means a < b and b < c, with b evaluated only once. Chaining works with any comparison operators, so 1 < 3 > 2 is True even though it reads oddly. Comparing incompatible types such as 3 < 'a' raises TypeError in Python 3, unlike Python 2.
points: 0 <= index < len(items) is the idiomatic range check.
== compares values, is compares identity, in tests membership.

theory.heading: Logical operators and short-circuiting
theory.body: and, or and not work on truthiness. and returns the first falsy operand or the last operand; or returns the first truthy operand or the last operand. Evaluation stops as soon as the result is known, which is called short-circuiting. That is why name = user_input or 'Guest' supplies a default, and why items and items[0] is safe for an empty list. not always returns a real bool.
points: Put cheap or guarding conditions first: if user and user.is_admin.

theory.heading: Bitwise operators
theory.body: &, |, ^, ~, << and >> operate on the binary representation of integers. They appear in interview questions about flags, permissions and tricks: n & 1 tests odd or even, n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit (so it is 0 exactly when a positive n is a power of two), x ^ x is 0 (used to find the single non-duplicated number), and n << k multiplies by 2 to the power k. ~n equals -n - 1 because Python ints behave like infinite two's complement.
points: Count set bits: bin(n).count('1') (or n.bit_count() in 3.10+).
a ^ b ^ a == b: XOR cancels pairs.

theory.heading: Precedence, assignment expressions and augmented assignment
theory.body: From highest to lowest the key levels are: ** ; unary - and ~ ; * / // % ; + - ; shifts ; & ; ^ ; | ; comparisons (including in and is) ; not ; and ; or ; the conditional expression ; and finally :=. When in doubt, add parentheses: readable code beats clever code. The walrus operator := (Python 3.8) assigns inside an expression, for example while (line := f.readline()):. Augmented assignment such as x += 1 may mutate in place for mutable types.
points: not a == b means not (a == b).
a if condition else b is Python's ternary expression.
Walrus avoids computing a value twice: if (n := len(data)) > 10: print(n).

example.title: Wrapping indices with modulo
example.body: Because % takes the sign of the divisor, moving backwards around a circular list never produces a negative index. This is a common trick in rotation and circular-buffer problems.

code.source:
days = ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun']
today = 1                       # Tue
print(days[(today - 3) % 7])    # Sat: (-2) % 7 == 5
print(days[(today + 10) % 7])   # Fri: 11 % 7 == 4
hours, minutes = divmod(135, 60)
print(hours, minutes)           # 2 15

use_cases.title: Defaults and guards
use_cases.description: or supplies fallback values and and guards attribute access on possibly-None objects.

use_cases.title: Permissions and flags
use_cases.description: Bitwise | combines flags and & tests them, as in file modes and feature toggles.

use_cases.title: Time and pagination maths
use_cases.description: divmod converts seconds into minutes and seconds or item counts into pages.

use_cases.title: Range validation
use_cases.description: Chained comparisons such as 18 <= age < 60 express business rules clearly.

demonstration.description: Evaluate a set of expressions whose results often surprise candidates.

takeaways: / always returns a float; // floors toward negative infinity.
% takes the sign of the divisor, so it wraps negative indices cleanly.
** is right-associative and binds tighter than unary minus.
and/or short-circuit and return one of their operands, not necessarily a bool.
n & (n - 1) == 0 (with n > 0) detects powers of two.
Use parentheses whenever precedence is not obvious to a reader.

interview.question: What is the difference between / and // in Python 3?
interview.answer: / is true division and always returns a float. // is floor division: it rounds the result down toward negative infinity, returning an int for int operands, so -7 // 2 is -4.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the negative-number behaviour separates a strong answer from a memorised one.

interview.question: What does 'a or b' return?
interview.answer: It returns a if a is truthy, otherwise b. It does not convert the result to a bool, and b is not evaluated when a is truthy.
interview.explanation: Link it to idioms such as name = value or 'default', and warn that 0 or '' are also replaced, which may be unintended.

interview.question: How do you check whether a number is a power of two without loops?
interview.answer: n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0. A power of two has exactly one set bit, and subtracting 1 flips that bit and all lower bits, so the AND is zero.
interview.explanation: Explaining why the trick works is more important than the formula itself.

interview.question: What does 1 < 3 > 2 evaluate to, and why?
interview.answer: True. Python chains comparisons, so it means 1 < 3 and 3 > 2, both of which are true.
interview.explanation: Shows you know chaining is a language feature, not left-to-right evaluation of booleans.

interview.question: What is the walrus operator and when would you use it?
interview.answer: The assignment expression := (Python 3.8) binds a name as part of an expression. It avoids repeating a computation, for example while (chunk := f.read(1024)): process(chunk) or [y for x in data if (y := f(x)) > 0].
interview.explanation: Mention it should be used where it improves clarity, not to cram logic into one line.

practice.title: Bitwise number inspector
practice.objective: Apply bitwise operators to answer classic questions about an integer's binary form.
practice.statement: For each non-negative integer, print: the number, its binary representation without the 0b prefix, the count of 1 bits, 'yes' or 'no' for whether it is a power of two (using n & (n - 1)), and 'even' or 'odd' decided with n & 1.
practice.input_format: The first line is N. The second line holds N space-separated non-negative integers.

example.output:
12 1100 2 no even
16 10000 1 yes even
7 111 3 no odd

constraints: 0 is not a power of two.
Use bitwise operators for the power-of-two and parity checks.
practice.starter:
n = int(input())
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
for v in values:
    # TODO: binary, number of ones, power of two, parity
    pass
practice.solution:
n = int(input())
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
for v in values:
    binary = bin(v)[2:]
    ones = binary.count('1')
    power = 'yes' if v > 0 and v & (v - 1) == 0 else 'no'
    parity = 'odd' if v & 1 else 'even'
    print(v, binary, ones, power, parity)
explanation: bin(v) returns a string such as '0b1100'; slicing [2:] removes the prefix.
Counting '1' characters gives the population count (int.bit_count() also works on 3.10+).
v & (v - 1) clears the lowest set bit; the result is 0 only when exactly one bit was set. The v > 0 guard excludes zero.
v & 1 is 1 for odd numbers because the lowest bit is set.

tests.output:
12 1100 2 no even
16 10000 1 yes even
7 111 3 no odd

quiz.question: What do the floor-division and modulo operators print?
quiz.explanation: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, giving -4. Then -7 - (-4 * 2) = 1, so the remainder is 1.

quiz.question: What does this exponent expression print?
quiz.explanation: ** is right-associative: 3 ** 2 is evaluated first (9), then 2 ** 9 = 512.

quiz.question: What do the or and and operators print?
quiz.explanation: or returns the first truthy operand ('default'); and returns the last operand when all are truthy (5).

quiz.question: user may be None. Which condition safely checks the user's is_admin attribute without raising AttributeError?
options: if user is not None and user.is_admin:
if user.is_admin and user is not None:
quiz.explanation: and short-circuits: when the first condition is False, user.is_admin is never evaluated.

quiz.question: What does the walrus operator := do?
options: Declares a constant that cannot be reassigned
Assigns a value to a name as part of a larger expression
quiz.explanation: The assignment expression, added in Python 3.8, binds a name and also evaluates to the value, e.g. while (line := f.readline()):.
